paper_title: Consistent Distribution Matching for Data-Free Diffusion Distillation

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Flow and diffusion models suffer from slow inference due to computationally expensive numerical integration. Distillation provides a promising way for a student model to learn from a teacher's dynamics, enabling one-step or few-step generation. However, existing methods often depend on curated distillation datasets, costly teacher rollouts, or auxiliary proxy networks, which complicate model training and scaling. In this work, we propose Consistent Distribution Matching, a simulation-free and data-free distillation method for accelerating diffusion and flow models while preserving strong generative capacity. Our key insight is to unify sample generation and score estimation with one student network. Thus, our framework uses only two models, a frozen teacher and a trainable student, and optimizes one objective. We prove that minimizing our objective indicates Wasserstein convergence of the student flow-map pushforwards to the teacher marginals. On ImageNet 256$\times$256, our method attains an FID of 2.04 with a single function evaluation (1-NFE) and a 4-NFE FID of 1.37 within 40 epochs of training, surpassing the state-of-the-art distillation baselines without data. Our code code and model are available at https://consistentdmd.github.io/.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Diffusion and flow-based generative models (Albergo et al., 2023; Lipman et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2023; Dhariwal & Nichol, 2021; Song et al., 2021; Karras et al., 2022; Ho et al., 2020; Rombach et al., 2022; Tong et al., 2025) have become leading framework for high-fidelity image and video synthesis. By learning continuous transport from simple prior distribution to complex data distribution, these models provide stable training and strong sample quality across wide spectrum of generative tasks (Fu et al., 2025; Yan et al., 2023; Wu et al., 2023b; Li et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025; Yan et al., 2025; Yin et al., 2025). Despite these advantages, their inference cost remains non-trivial. The primary bottleneck lies in the iterative denoising procedure during inference. Generating single sample requires numerically solving the differential equations governing the generative dynamics, which often involves hundreds of neural function evaluations. 1 Figure 2: Curated 10241024 samples produced by our 4-step CDMD generator distilled from SANA1.6B LORA (Xie et al., 2024a). Please zoom in for details. To address this challenge, diffusion distillation (Geng et al., 2024; Song et al., 2023; Song & Dhariwal, 2023; Lu & Song, 2024; Meng et al., 2023; Frans et al., 2024; Sabour et al., 2025; Fu et al., 2025) provides natural route to accelerate the generation with new model. Given powerful teacher diffuser, the student is trained to reproduce the teachers generative behavior while compressing the inference process in one or few steps. Existing distillation methods have made substantial progress, yet their training pipelines often introduce additional complexity. Some depend on heavy backward simulation (Liu et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2026; Gu et al., 2023) of teacher diffusion model, auxiliary fake score networks (Yin et al., 2024b;a; Xie et al., 2024b; Zhou et al., 2024; 2025d; Luo et al., 2025; Ge et al., 2026), adversarial objectives (Zhou et al., 2025d; Kim et al., 2023; Sauer et al., 2024; 2025), or multi-stage training (Lee et al., 2024). Although these components enable high-quality generation in few steps, they incur substantial memory overhead, impose an egregiously high optimization burden, and ultimately hinder the scalability of the distillation procedure. Beyond this procedural complexity, reliance on external distillation data (Yin et al., 2024b;a; Peng et al., 2025; Song et al., 2023; Lu & Song, 2024; Meng et al., 2023; Zhou et al., 2024) introduces fundamental source of mismatch between data and teacher probability path. Data-based methods construct intermediate states by noising real data samples, often drawn from distillation dataset that differs from the data used to train the teacher. Consequently, these states may deviate from those actually visited by the teacher during generation, causing the student to be supervised on surrogate state distribution, instead of along the teachers probability path. This mismatch of the supervision states (Tong et al., 2025) becomes pronounced when fine-tuning tilts the teachers distribution away from the original data (Xie et al., 2024b; Chen et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2025) or when the teacher adopts classifier-free guidance (Ho & Salimans, 2022) or autoguidance (Karras et al., 2024). In these settings, noising samples from the original data distribution provides progressively less faithful coverage of the states visited by the teacher. Moreover, when teacher model is trained on proprietary data (Rombach et al., 2022; Wu et al., 2025; Seedream et al., 2025; Labs, 2025), constructing such data-anchored supervision path may be infeasible. Direct supervision on teacher trajectories would address the mismatch, but obtaining such states requires backward simulation, thereby reintroducing the aforementioned computational burden. This trade-off motivates our central question: can we distill diffusion or flow teacher into few-step student without external data, teacher rollouts, or auxiliary fake score models? We propose Consistent Distribution Matching Distillation (CDMD), data-free and simulation-free framework for distilling diffusion and flow models using only frozen teacher and trainable student. Our framework aims to circumvent the distribution mismatch issues. Our central idea is to unify 2 sample generation and score estimation within single flow map model, eliminating the need for separately trained proxy network. The student predicts average velocities over arbitrary denoising time intervals, supporting generation in one or few steps. We bootstrap intermediate training states from student predictions and analytic forward noising, avoiding real data and teacher rollouts while allowing the training distribution to evolve with the student. Although these states do not necessarily coincide with those visited by the teacher during generation, our objective progressively aligns the corresponding student probability path with the teacher probability path. This enables the teacher to provide corrective velocity supervision directly on states relevant to the students generative dynamics. At these states, we regress the student velocity surrogate toward the teachers instantaneous velocity through single objective. Moreover, as the states become noisier, they increasingly resemble the distributions encountered during teacher training, making the teachers velocity supervision more reliable. This trend is consistently observed across existing distribution matching baselines (Yin et al., 2024a;b). The quality of the supervision also improves as the student distribution moves closers to the teacher distribution. We further establish theoretical connection between local transport consistency and distribution matching. Under appropriate assumptions, minimizing population loss implies that the distributions induced by the student flow map converge to the teacher marginals in squared Wasserstein-2 distance averaged over time. Importantly, this result does not require the supervision states to be sampled from the teachers probability path. Next, the minimizer of our objective becomes the teacher average velocity. Overall, these results explain how local consistency can identify the teachers transport behavior and achieve distributional alignment without auxiliary score networks. Our contributions are threefold: 1. We introduce Consistent Distribution Matching Distillation, data-free and simulation-free distillation framework for diffusion and flow-based generative models. The method uses only frozen teacher and trainable student, avoiding external distillation data, teacher rollouts and auxiliary proxy networks. 2. We provide distribution-matching analysis showing that minimizing the proposed CDMD objective leads to narrowing the gap between the teacher distribution and the student distribution under regularity assumptions. The analysis also identifies the teachers average velocity field as the unique global minimizer for our objective. 3. We analyze the variance of the JVP correction in the data-free setting and validate the analysis on synthetic datasets. These results clarify when the correction improves stability and when student-teacher path mismatch can degrade training. On ImageNet256256, Consistent Distribution Matching Distillation achieves 1-NFE FID of 2.04 and 4-NFE FID of 1.37, achieving state-of-the-art performance among data-free distillation methods. In the text-to-image comparison when training data is inaccessible, our method leads most preference and alignment metrics and FID.

sections.title: 5 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Trajectory Distillation. Distillation accelerates diffusion sampling by training students to reproduce the teachers dynamics in fewer steps. Knowledge distillation (Zheng et al., 2023) learns direct mapping from noise to data, while progressive distillation (Salimans & Ho, 2022; Meng et al., 2023) repeatedly halves the number of sampling steps. Consistency models (Lu & Song, 2024; Song & Dhariwal, 2023; Song et al., 2023; Luo et al., 2023a) map states along the same ODE trajectory to shared clean sample. Flow map distillation (Boffi et al., 2025; Geng et al., 2025a;b; Sabour et al., 2025; Lee et al., 2026) extends this idea to transitions between arbitrary times along trajectory. BOOT (Gu et al., 2023), π-Flow (Chen et al., 2025), and rectified flow (Liu et al., 2023) explore 9 ways to reduce reliance on real training data. For methods that require teacher reference trajectories, generating them during training or precomputing them can limit scalability as tasks become more complex. Our method avoids numerically integrating the teacher during training. Compared with FreeFlow (Tong et al., 2025), which anchors its flow map at noise, our model supports transitions from arbitrary input states and times.

sections.title: 6 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We presented CDMD, data-free and simulation-free framework for distilling pretrained diffusion and flow-based teachers into efficient one-step or few-step flow map students. Our method eliminates the need for external distillation data, teacher rollouts, backward simulation, and auxiliary proxy networks by training on student-induced distribution with single objective. Motivated by the velocity form Theoretically, we showed that, under regularity assumptions, minimizing our CDMD objective leads to convergence of student sampling distributions to teacher distributions in Wasserstein distance, averaged over reference times, and every global minimizer recovers the teacher average velocity on sampled states. Empirically, CDMD achieves state-of-the-art ImageNet256256 generation quality among data-free distillation methods and further benefits from inference-time scaling through its parameterization. Our method also achieves the best overall performance in text-to-image generation, leading on both preference and alignment metrics as well as image-quality metrics. These results suggest that strong data-free distillation can be achieved with simpler two-model training pipeline, while preserving the flexibility of multi-step sampling. Future work includes improving the stability of the JVP term, developing initialization strategies when no model weights are available, and extending the framework to large-scale generative tasks where data scarcity problem dominates.

sections.content: Tab. 4 compares representative distillation methods by the number of networks and optimizers they need, and by whether they require real data, trajectory simulation, or an adversarial objective. DMD2, SiD-LSG, SiDA, FreeFlow, and CTM train third auxiliary network, either fake-score model or discriminator, with second optimizer. BOOT is data-free but simulates trajectories during training. FACM and the flow map models (MF, CM, IMM) use only two networks and one optimizer, but they construct noisy states from real data. CDMD is the only method in the table that is both data-free and simulation-free while keeping only the teacher, the student, and single optimizer. The subsections below relate CDMD to FreeFlow, flow maps, and DMD in more detail. sections.title: D IMPLEMENTATION DETAILS
sections.content: This section gives the training, architecture, and evaluation details for class-conditional ImageNet (Appendix D.1), the analytic 2D benchmarks behind Fig. 5 (Appendix D.2), and the SANA-1.6B text-to-image setting (Appendix D.3). D.1 CLASS-CONDITIONAL IMAGENET Training-state construction. Fig. 7(a) shows the two data-free constructions of ˆxt in Eq. (6). In the upper construction (s = t), the student jumps from the prior sample x1 directly to each intermediate time, e.g., ˆxt = fθ(x1, 1, t), so the training state lies on the student path. In the lower construction (s = 0), the student first produces clean sample ˆx0 = fθ(x1, 1, 0), which is then re-noised along the conditional flow path with fresh Gaussian noise. Each construction costs one student evaluation and no teacher rollout. Fig. 7(b) shows the supervision on such state: the student average velocity uθ( ˆxt, t, r) defines the jump ˆxt fθ( ˆxt, t, r) over [r, t], and its corrected velocity is regressed onto the teacher velocity v( ˆxt, t). In Alg. 1, z1 and z2 are the = 0 and = states, respectively. They are mixed with ratio (Tab. 2) and detached before the teacher is queried. Training. The backbone architectures follow SiT, which is based on DiT (Peebles & Xie, 2023) with adaLN-Zero (Peebles & Xie, 2023) for conditioning. To condition the student model on the additional variables, we use two-layer SiLU-activated MLP whose hidden dimension matches the models hidden dimension. We add new embeddings for and w, and adopt adaLN-Zero for conditioning. The resulting conditioning signal is fed to each transformer block. No further architectural changes are necessary for stable and effective training. Note that SiT teacher and SiT+VA-REPA have different configurations on what the time in FM represents. SiT adopts the convention when x1 pdata, x0 pprior which is the opposite of the notion we adopt in this paper. Our convention on FM time aligns with SiT+VA-REPA (Yang et al., 2026) or SiT+REPA (Yu et al., 2024) in their implementation. Our training algorithm strictly follows 1. In addition, we use Flash-Attention to reduce GPU memory usage and accelerate training. Plus, we customize the Flash-Attention kernel to support JVP computation, following sCM (Lu & Song, 2024). All models are trained using the PyTorch framework. The detailed training hyperparameters are provided in Tab. 5. Architecture. We evaluate on an analytic 2D spiral benchmark, where the teacher velocity field and target distribution are available in closed form, without relying on learned teacher checkpoint. As shown in Fig. 8, samples are transported from Gaussian prior at = 1 to spiral target distribution at = 0. This controlled low-dimensional setting allows us to evaluate not only the terminal marginal distribution but also the learned transport behavior. Both methods use the same one-step student architecture and evaluation protocol. We compare our training objective directly against the FreeFlow objective. The converged-state results in Table 6 show that matching the terminal marginal alone is insufficient to characterize distillation quality: although both methods achieve essentially the same final W2 score, our objective learns substantially more accurate average velocity field and better coupled transport map. Concretely, CDMD reduces the error to the ground-truth average velocity from 0.317 to 0.070 and the coupled = 1 endpoint error from 0.0316 to 0.0040, while both methods reach W2 = 0.190. In addition to the spiral, we use 2D checkerboard target with the same protocol for the JVP diagnostics below. Figure 9 compares the projected JVP variance VJVP and the cross-centered second moment Mq,p JVP for the three candidate tangent directions on the 2D checkerboard (Figure 9a) and spiral (Figure 9b) datasets. Across both datasets, evaluating the JVP along the teacher tangent, ˆxt/dt = v( ˆxt, t), consistently yields the smallest and most stable correction statistics throughout training. The local student tangent, uθ( ˆxt, t, t), results in modest increase in both quantities, whereas the global one-step student displacement, uθ(z, 1, 0), exhibits substantially larger variability and an increasing trend over training. This difference is particularly pronounced on the spiral dataset, where the global displacement remains well separated from the two state-local tangent choices. Moreover, the projected variance and cross-centered second moment exhibit nearly identical trends and rankings, suggesting that the cross-distribution contribution is relatively small in these experiments and that the observed differences are primarily driven by the intrinsic stochasticity of the JVP correction. These results support using the teacher velocity v( ˆxt, t) as the JVP input direction when constructing the detached correction target. 27 (a) Results on the 2D checkerboard dataset. Every time we construct the intermediate states we start with the nearest earlier teacher checkpoint and we add noise according to the forward path. ABLATION ON INFERENCE-TIME SCALING F.1 SAMPLER COMPARISON WITH THE SIT-XL/2+VA-REPA TEACHER We further study inference-time scaling by comparing Euler, Heun, and DDIM samplers under different classifier-free guidance scales. Figure 11 reports FID as function of the number of sampling steps for = 1.5 and = 2.0. In some literatures (Lee et al., 2026; Song et al., 2023), DDIM method has also been referred as the Restart sampler. The ablation suggests that increasing the inference-time sampling budget does not automatically improve our distilled model. DDIM gives the strongest low-step performance in both guidance settings and remains especially stable from one to four steps. Euler is competitive at one or two steps for = 1.5, but its FID increases as more steps are used and then plateaus. Heun is the least stable in the low-step regime: it exhibits sharp FID spike at two steps and only recovers after additional steps. The effect is more pronounced under stronger guidance, where both Euler and Heun drift to noticeably worse FID than DDIM as the sampling budget grows. 30 These results give useful guidance for scaling inference time in our model. The interval-conditioned parameterization supports multi-step sampling, but the benefit depends strongly on the sampler and guidance scale. In this setting, DDIM is the most reliable choice for converting extra inference steps into stable sample quality, while higher-order or updates can amplify student-teacher mismatch at small step counts. We attribute this behavior primarily to these two factors. First, our training schedule assigns substantial probability mass to intervals with = r, which may make the learned update less compatible with aggressive higher-order extrapolation at inference time. Second, the quality of the teacher, particularly its performance without CFG, has pronounced effect on the distilled model. Empirically, we observe that differences in teacher performance without CFG translate into differences in the final student performance. Note that this student is trained with = for only 10% of the pairs (Tab. 5). Appendix F.2 tests the first factor with student trained with = for 50% of the pairs. F.2 INFERENCE-TIME SCALING WITH THE LIGHTNINGDIT-XL/2 TEACHER Fig. 12 repeats the inference-time scaling study for the student distilled from LightningDiT-XL/2. We sample the same student with Euler and DDIM from 1 to 64 steps without retraining. Unlike the SiT-XL/2+VA-REPA student in Fig. 11, the Euler FID decreases from 2.04 at 1 step to 1.62 at 2 steps and 1.37 at 4 steps (Tab. 1), and reaches its minimum at 8 steps. From 8 to 64 steps, the Euler FID stays nearly flat and close to the teacher reference instead of drifting upward. The Euler IS rises from about 294 at 1 step to about 320 at 16 steps and then saturates. Additional steps thus refine the samples, as they do for the teacher FM model, and never cause the large degradation of the 10% = student. The main difference between the two students is the training schedule. The LightningDiT student samples = for 50% of the pairs, whereas the SiT-XL/2+VA-REPA student in Fig. 11 uses 10% (Tab. 5). On = pairs, the objective reduces to uθ( ˆxt, t, t) v( ˆxt, t)2, so the student directly learns the teacher instantaneous velocity, which governs small sampling steps. This result matches Fig. 6b in the main text, where raising the fraction of = pairs from 10% to 50% substantially reduces the multi-step degradation (FID about 5.1 instead of 9.8 at 50 steps). Since the same behavior appears with different teacher, the stability is property of the and schedule rather than of particular teacher: keeping = for 50% of the pairs is enough to preserve the multi-step behavior of the teacher as the number of sampling steps increases, while still giving the best 1-NFE FID in Tab. 1. DDIM behaves differently. Its FID is close to Euler at 1 and 2 steps but rises steadily after 4 steps and exceeds 5 at 64 steps, while its IS grows monotonically to above 420. Rising IS together with rising FID indicates that DDIM increasingly trades sample diversity for class fidelity as the number of steps grows. For this student, Euler is therefore the preferred sampler for inference-time scaling.

sections.title: H LIMITATIONS AND BROADER IMPACT
sections.content: A key limitation of the current formulation is the absence of meaningful constraints on the total derivative term dt u(xt, t, r) = v(xt, t)Dxtu+tu. To date, this component has not been rigorously analyzed. In prior work, it is typically detached from the computational graph and excluded from backpropagation, effectively treating it as constant. However, empirical observations reveal that its norm is large and fluctuates substantially throughout training, suggesting that this simplification may be problematic. plausible direction for regularization is to leverage well-trained reference velocity field v(xt, t), encouraging the derivative term to exhibit similar, more stable behavior. In practice, not only is the dataset private, but the teacher model weights are also inaccessible. Hence, we cannot initialize the student model with the teacher model weights, which is common practice in distillation work. This makes training more challenging and less stable. Moreover, we speculate that for different tasks, the way we bootstrapped our xt is of great importance. This can substantially influence the learning dynamics and overall effectiveness of distillation. I
